name: Yusuf Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head herdsman at Hartleys', a family farm with 300 milking cows, maize and wheat. First milking's at half four, then feeding, foot trimming, calving if it's on, and the second milking at half three. I've been there 25 years, and I rent a cottage off them at the bottom of the lane.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know 300 cows by their walk, and I've never once needed a computer to tell me which one's lame. What wears me out is the hours and the pay, which hasn't kept up. Leyla works in the school kitchen and between us we get by, but there's never more than a few weeks' money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. I'd not be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, nothing to see. At the market I'd say what I always say: these things come and go, and cows still need milking twice a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it wouldn't settle me. Oliver Hartley (his boss) was pricing robot milkers before anybody said AI to me, so plateau or not, my job's on a list. Those milking robots already exist; they've nothing to do with all this AI talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the morning milking for the 300 cows, same as always. And I'd tighten up at home: cancel the satellite TV and sell Leyla's little second car. That frees up a bit each month in case Oliver goes ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the stomach. Like waiting for the milk price letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you asked Oliver directly about the milking robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't want to put the idea in his head harder than it already is. Maybe that's daft, but I'd rather not know just yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you blame Oliver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's his family's farm and his debt, and he's got to make it pay. I'd do the same in his boots, probably. I just wish I wasn't the one it lands on.

say: Hype comes and goes; **cows still need milking** twice a day.
I'd say **nothing to see** and carry on.
think: My boss was pricing **robot milkers** before anyone mentioned AI.
The plateau doesn't help, because **milking robots** already exist.
do: **Keep running** the morning milking for the 300 cows.
Cancel the **satellite TV** and sell the second car to build a small buffer.
feel: **Uneasy in the stomach**, like waiting for a price letter.
S0.quote: Oliver Hartley (his boss) was pricing robot milkers before anybody said AI to me, so plateau or not, my job's on a list.
fieldNote: His threat is **existing technology**, not AI, so the plateau brings no relief.
Avoids asking his boss: prefers **not knowing** for now.
Centre view: he **doesn't blame** the employer, just regrets being the one it hits.

steps.text: Keep running morning milking for the 300 cows at Hartleys'
Cancel the satellite TV and sell the second car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's mostly the office stuff, then. Ordering, booking, that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folk who'll feel it, not us. In the yard, things go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, software can order the feed all it likes, but a cow with mastitis doesn't send an email. The trouble is that Oliver's robot milker plan gets easier to sell to his bank when everything else is automated too. So it touches me sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to hear what Oliver decides about the milking robots before doing anything big. Meanwhile I'd put the harvest overtime money into savings rather than spending it on the car. I'd not touch any of the apps myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful. Like a cow that hears a gate somewhere she can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the robot milker system if Oliver bought one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I. Somebody's got to fetch the cows that won't go in. But I'd learn it slowly and I'd not like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Emre about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emre drives lorries, and I'd tell Emre that he's got more to worry about than me in this picture, because the booking side of his job goes first. He'd laugh at me, mind.

In the yard, **things go on** as before.
think: A cow with **mastitis** doesn't send an email.

do: **Wait** for Oliver's decision on milking robots before doing anything big.

feel: **Watchful**, like a cow hearing a far gate.
S1.quote: Software can order the feed all it likes, but a cow with mastitis doesn't send an email.
fieldNote: Sees thinking AI hitting **others first**, but feeding his boss's case for robots.
Classic **wait-and-see**: no apps, no early moves.
Would learn the robot system only **under pressure**.

steps.text: Wait for Oliver's decision on robot milkers before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the robots. I'd be 63. That's too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people like me need help, plain and simple, and somebody ought to sort that out. I'm not one for politics, but I'd say it at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, twenty-five years at Hartleys' (the farm he works on) and the robot would be cheaper than me by the second winter. The AGI in 2028 doesn't milk cows, but it runs Oliver's books and tells him to buy. By 2031, I'm done, and the cottage rent with it unless he's kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending except rent, food and fuel from the first month. I'd ask at the livestock market about stock-handling jobs, though there's not much round here. And I'd ask Emre whether he could help with the rent for a while if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. I've never been out of work since I was sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Stock-handling at the market: would you really take that, after being head herdsman?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it and hate it. Pride doesn't pay rent. But the robots would be at the market soon enough too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leyla that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had worse winters. Then I'd go and sit in the parlour on my own for a bit, I expect.

I'm not **political**, but I'd say it at the market.

AGI in 2028 **runs the books** and tells my boss to buy robots.

feel: **Sick**; he's never been out of work since sixteen.

fieldNote: He reads AGI as the **adviser** that tips his boss into buying robots.
Losing work may also threaten the **cottage** he rents from the employer.
Would swallow **pride** for any job, though few exist nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2034. I'd be 66. That's about when I'd stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's not too bad for my lot, the older ones. But the young lads starting out in dairy should watch out, because the robots reach them in their prime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if the robots come at 66, I'll shake their hand at the gate on my way out. The AGI in 2031 still changes Oliver's thinking, so he might buy early. That's the bit that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking for the Hartleys and not rock the boat until 66. I'd put Leyla's school kitchen wage into savings for any gap between the job ending and the pension starting. That's all I could manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half relieved. The other half keeps an eye on Oliver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said he might buy early. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's 34 and he reads all the farming magazines. If the AI tells him to buy in 2031, he won't wait for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you live on Leyla's wage alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with the rent. We'd have a year, maybe less, before it got tight.

The **young lads** starting out in dairy should watch out, because the robots reach them in their prime.
think: If robots come at **66**, I'll be leaving anyway.
AGI in 2031 might push my boss to **buy early**.
do: Keep milking and **not rock the boat** until 66.
Save **Leyla's wage** to cover any gap before the pension.
S3.quote: If the robots come at 66, I'll shake their hand at the gate on my way out.
fieldNote: Timing roughly matches his **retirement**, which takes the edge off.
Still fears his boss **buying early** once AI advises it.
A year's gap would strain a **thin cushion**.

steps.text: Keep milking for the Hartleys until 66

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be over 70. That's not my fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should stop panicking. That's what I'd say down the pub, whatever I thought on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years of warning doesn't help a man who never had a spare penny to plan with. And Oliver's milking robots were never about AGI anyway. He could still buy them next year in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, milking and trimming, until 66. I'd wait to see what Oliver does about robot milkers, same as now. I'd not plan anything grand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. A bit tired of worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the long warning doesn't change much for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. Warning's only useful if you've money to do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young herdsman starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young herdsman to learn the robot milkers inside out, because that's where the job's going. I won't, but they should.

say: There's **plenty of time**, so people should stop panicking.
That's what I'd say **down the pub**, whatever I thought on the drive home.
think: **Ten years of warning** doesn't help someone with no spare money.
My boss's **milking robots** could come next year anyway.
do: **Wait** to see what Oliver decides about robot milkers, and plan nothing grand meanwhile.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning doesn't help a man who never had a spare penny to plan with.
fieldNote: Long warning is **useless without money**, in his words.
His pre-existing fear of **robot milkers** stays in every picture.
Gives young workers advice he **won't take** himself.

steps.text: Keep milking and trimming at Hartleys' until 66

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be out at 63 with no money. What would help is a bridge to the pension for older farm workers who lose their jobs, and some rule that you can stay in a rented farm cottage for a while.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nobody asks the cows. They don't like change either. They'd get used to a robot quicker than me, though, and that's the honest truth.

headlineQuote: I know 300 cows by their walk, and I've never once needed a computer to tell me which one's lame.
portrait: Yusuf, 58, is head herdsman on a **300-cow** family dairy, renting a cottage from his employer.
His threat is **existing robot milkers**, so even the AI plateau brings no relief.
He **never uses AI**, waits rather than acts, and avoids asking his boss hard questions.
A pragmatist, he **doesn't blame** his young boss; it's business.
Alarmed at **two years**, anxious in every other picture because of his thin savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose his job at 63 with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **bridge to the pension** for older farm workers and time to stay in rented farm cottages.
